per_question.question: Who is allowed to work on energized electrical parts and how must circuits be deenergized?
per_question.system_answer: Only qualified persons may work on electric circuit parts or equipment that have not been deenergized under the procedures of paragraph (b) of this section. (A) Installation, removal, or repair of lines energized at more than 600 volts, (B) Installation, removal, or repair of deenergized lines if an employee is exposed to contact with other parts energized at more than 600 volts, (C) Installation, removal, or repair of equipment, such as transformers, capacitors, and regulators, if an employee is exposed to contact with parts energized at more than 600 volts, (D) Work involving the use of mechanical equipment, other than insulated aerial lifts, near parts energized at more than 600 volts, and Such persons shall be capable of working safely on energized circuits and shall be familiar with the proper use of special precautionary techniques, personal protective equipment, insulating and shielding materials, and insulated tools. (i) Only qualified employees may work on or with exposed energized lines or parts of equipment.
per_question.golden_answer: Only qualified persons may work on exposed energized parts. Circuits must be deenergized before work when possible, locked or tagged out, and verified deenergized by a qualified person; energized work is allowed only when permitted by the standard.

per_question.question: Fire prevention precautions before welding or cutting near combustibles
per_question.system_answer: Cutting or welding shall be permitted only in areas that are or have been made fire safe. per_question.golden_answer: Before welding or cutting near combustibles, remove or protect combustibles within 35 feet, inspect the opposite side of walls and floors, provide suitable fire extinguishing equipment, and assign a fire watch when required.

per_question.question: Requirements for flammable liquid storage cabinets
per_question.system_answer: Not more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids, nor more than 120 gallons of Category 4 flammable liquids may be stored in a storage cabinet. Cabinets shall be labeled in conspicuous lettering, “Flammable—Keep Fire Away.” Storage cabinets shall be designed and constructed to limit the internal temperature to not more than 325 °F. when subjected to a 10-minute fire test using the standard time-temperature curve as set forth in Standard Methods of Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials, NFPA 251-1969, which is incorporated by reference as specified in § 1910.6. Original closed containers, approved portable tanks, approved safety cans or a properly arranged system of piping shall be used for bringing flammable liquids or liquids with a flashpoint greater than 199.4 °F (93 °C) into spray finishing room.
per_question.golden_answer: Not more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids, nor more than 120 gallons of Category 4 flammable liquids, may be stored in a storage cabinet.

per_question.question: When should danger tags and caution signs be used?
per_question.system_answer: Warning tags may be used to represent a hazard level between “Caution” and “Danger,” instead of the required “Caution” tag, provided that they have a signal word of “Warning,” an appropriate major message, and otherwise meet the general tag criteria of paragraph (f)(4) of this section. Danger tags shall be used only in these situations. Danger tags shall be used in major hazard situations where an immediate hazard presents a threat of death or serious injury to employees. Caution tags shall be used only in these situations. Caution tags shall be used in minor hazard situations where a non-immediate or potential hazard or unsafe practice presents a lesser threat of employee injury.
per_question.golden_answer: Use danger signs for an immediate hazard that presents a serious threat of death or serious injury. Use caution signs for a potential hazard or unsafe practice that may result in minor or moderate injury.
